RESEARCH TASK for Kodely, an AI website builder (codebase at C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod). Deliverable is analysis, not code.

## Why
The planning board has a "Competitor Teardowns" column with **99 cards** — the single largest research block on it, and by far the least actionable in its current form. Individual observations about Lovable, Bolt.new, v0, Replit, Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Base44, Rocket.new and others, with no synthesis. Nobody can act on 99 cards.

Your job is to turn that pile into decisions.

## Read the board first
The board is a SQLite database at `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Kodely\Kodely Board\board.sqlite` (`node:sqlite`, `DatabaseSync`). **READ ONLY — do not write to it.**

Table shapes: `boards(id,name,position)`, `columns(id,boardId,name,position)`, `cards(id,columnId,title,description,phase,type,priority,labels,assignee,position,archivedAt,createdAt)`.

The Kodely Research board id is `720aa8c1-d259-4e49-b777-c58965efabd1`. Pull every card in the "Competitor Teardowns" column and read the descriptions, not just the titles — the substance is in the descriptions.

## Then ground it in what Kodely actually is
- `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM prompt in full, `lib/foundation.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**` (the CSP — no external requests, no backend), `lib/credits.ts` and `lib/stripe.ts` (pricing and real margins), `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts` (zip export, built but not deployed).
- Kodely today generates **single-page** React sites with **no backend, no database, no auth, no forms that deliver, no custom domains, no uploaded images**. Every comparison must respect that.

## Also verify current reality
Competitor pricing and capabilities move fast and the board cards may be stale. Use WebSearch/WebFetch to check the important claims. **Where you cannot verify something, say so explicitly rather than repeating a board card as fact.**

## Deliver two things

**1. A synthesis document** at `docs/research/competitive-position.md`:
- Where Kodely genuinely wins today, with the code that backs each claim.
- Where it structurally cannot compete right now, and what would have to change.
- The pricing landscape and where Kodely's packs sit (starter 500 credits/$9, builder 2500/$40, pro 6000/$90, ~87-89% gross margin against a $0.002/credit cost basis).
- The 3-5 strategic choices this analysis actually forces.
- Which board cards are now STALE or WRONG, listed explicitly with what changed.

**2. A JSON array** at `C:\Users\edmem\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-edmem-OneDrive-Desktop-Kodely\eb67eaec-3d5e-420f-a5fc-4419d7203aa9\scratchpad\cards-competitive.json`

Each element: `{"title": "...", "description": "...", "type": "FEATURE"|"CHORE"|"IDEA"|"BUG", "priority": "LOW"|"NORMAL"|"HIGH"|"URGENT", "labels": ["..."]}`

**15-25 cards maximum** — this is a distillation, not another pile. Each card must be a decision or an action, with the reasoning in the description. If your output is 25 more observations, you have failed the task.

## Constraints
- **Write ONLY those two files.** No code, no schema, no config, and absolutely no writes to `board.sqlite`.
- Do not invent competitor pricing, funding, user counts or capabilities. Verify or state that you could not.
- Be fair and factual about competitors — no disparagement, and no claiming a Kodely advantage that the code does not support.
- Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.

## Report back
Kodely's real defensible position in two sentences, the 3-5 forced strategic choices, how many of the 99 cards you found stale, and how many cards you wrote.

1	=== #0 [IDEA/HIGH] What rocket.new is: "Vibe Solutioning" platform
2	["research"]
3	Rocket.new positions itself as the "world's first Vibe Solutioning platform" — not just an AI app builder. It bundles three pillars into one shared-context workspace: **Solve** (market research, idea validation, PRDs, competitor mapping), **Build** (generate production-ready web + mobile apps), and **Intelligence** (continuous 24/7 competitor monitoring, daily briefings). This 'strategy-before-code' framing is its core differentiator vs. Lovable/Bolt, which jump straight to generation. Source: https://www.rocket.new/ and https://docs.rocket.new/getting-started/introduction
4	
5	=== #1 [IDEA/NORMAL] Company: DhiWise → Rocket pivot, $15M seed
6	["research"]
7	Rocket.new is the rebrand of **DhiWise**, founded April 2021 in Surat, India by Vishal Virani, Rahul Shingala, and Deepak Dhanak. DhiWise raised ~$9.5M (Series A led by Accel). It rebranded to Rocket in **September 2025**, went AI-first, relocated HQ to Palo Alto, and raised a **$15M seed** led by Salesforce Ventures with Accel, India Quotient, and Together Fund. Sources: https://techcrunch.com/2022/08/22/dhiwise-takes-the-tedium-out-of-programming/ , https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/dhiwise
8	
9	=== #2 [IDEA/HIGH] Traction signals: 400K users, 500K apps, $4.5M ARR
10	["research"]
11	Within ~3 months of the June 2025 beta launch Rocket reportedly crossed **400,000+ users** across **180 countries**, generated **500,000+ applications**, hit **$4.5M ARR** with **10,000+ paid subscribers**. Enterprise logos claimed include Meta, PayPal, KPMG, and PwC. These are self-reported PR numbers — treat with caution, but they indicate fast growth Kodely is competing against. Source: https://www.producthunt.com/stories/from-golden-kitty-to-10m-raised and productgrowth.in review
12	
13	=== #3 [IDEA/HIGH] Workflow: prompt → full-stack app in one shot
14	["research"]
15	Rocket treats every prompt as a **full-stack build instruction** — a single natural-language prompt (or Figma frame / screenshot / Notion doc) generates screens, navigation, data model, and design together, aiming to avoid iterative rounds ('one-shot' mode). It then generates frontend + backend + DB schema + auth + API endpoints + file storage simultaneously. Users iterate afterward via chat or the visual editor. Source: https://www.rocket.new/ai-app-builder and https://www.rocket.new/blog/best-ai-prompts-for-one-shot-app-generation-guide-this-year
16	
17	=== #4 [IDEA/HIGH] Generated tech stack: Next.js web, Flutter mobile, Supabase
18	["research"]
19	Web apps are generated as **Next.js (React/TypeScript)**; mobile apps as **Flutter** (iOS + Android). The default backend is **Supabase** — bundling PostgreSQL, auth (email/password + Google/GitHub social), row-level security, file storage, and edge functions. Auth, DB schemas, and REST endpoints are auto-generated. This opinionated stack is a key contrast point for Kodely's own stack choice. Sources: https://docs.rocket.new/integrations/supabase , https://www.rocket.new/build
20	
21	=== #5 [IDEA/HIGH] Deploys to Netlify (third-party hosting dependency)
22	["research"]
23	Despite marketing 'Rocket-hosted infrastructure', the docs reveal web apps actually deploy to **Netlify** with a public URL via the 'Launch' button, and **custom domains require connecting your own Netlify account**. Mobile builds get a mobile-optimized web preview link. This reliance on external hosting is a strategic opening for Kodely, which owns its VPS/hosting stack and can offer first-party hosting. Source: https://docs.rocket.new/help/faq
24	
25	=== #6 [IDEA/HIGH] Trustpilot: 3.3/5 across ~60 reviews (polarized)
26	["research"]
27	Rocket.new holds a **TrustScore of 3.3/5 from ~60 reviews** on Trustpilot — 'Average', notably lower than typical SaaS. Experiences are highly polarized: praise for bringing ideas to life fast and helpful support, versus complaints about cost and bugs. The mediocre score despite huge user numbers signals real retention/satisfaction risk. Source: https://www.trustpilot.com/review/rocket.new
28	
29	=== #7 [IDEA/URGENT] #1 Complaint: credits burn fast, builds get expensive
30	["research"]
31	The dominant complaint across Trustpilot/reviews: **credits are consumed very quickly** and building a fully functional app routinely requires buying extra credits. One user reported spending **$250 on credits**; testimonials cite ~**200k 'credits' for a mobile app build**. Non-technical users report 'credits running out before meaningful features ship', making cost unpredictable. This is the single biggest wedge for Kodely to undercut. Source: https://www.trustpilot.com/review/rocket.new
32	
33	=== #8 [IDEA/URGENT] #2 Complaint: fixing Rocket's own bugs costs more credits
34	["research"]
35	Reviewers describe the platform as 'half-baked' with unstable workflows: prompting it to fix an issue often introduces new problems, and **fixing bugs the platform itself created consumes additional credits**. This 'pay-to-fix-its-own-mistakes' loop is the most damaging recurring criticism. Kodely should design so error correction / self-heal iterations are cheap or free. Source: https://www.trustpilot.com/review/rocket.new
36	
37	=== #9 [IDEA/NORMAL] Strength: pre-build 'Solve' intelligence layer
38	["research"]
39	Rocket's genuine differentiator is the **Solve phase** that runs before code: market research, competitive landscape mapping, problem validation, and a structured strategic brief (exportable as PDF/PPTX). Competitors (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) have no equivalent strategy/research layer. If Kodely competes purely on build, this is where Rocket claims an edge worth neutralizing or matching. Source: https://www.rocket.new/blog/rocket-new-vs-bolt-vs-replit-the-difference-that-precedes-build-over-code-quality
40	
41	=== #10 [IDEA/NORMAL] Strength: 'production-grade' code you own + Intelligence
42	["research"]
43	Rocket markets clean, production-grade code that 'belongs entirely to you', with SEO optimization, accessibility, responsive layouts, and modular architecture built into the first generation — positioning against Lovable/Bolt as 'apps not prototypes'. The **Intelligence** pillar (ongoing competitor monitoring + daily briefings) is a retention/recurring-value hook competitors lack. Source: https://www.rocket.new/blog/rocket-new-vs-lovable-which-builds-production-ready-apps-not-prototypes
44	
45	=== #11 [IDEA/NORMAL] Positioning vs Lovable / Bolt / Replit
46	["research"]
47	In head-to-heads Rocket frames rivals as fast but shallow: Lovable = fast build, no pre-build intelligence/memory; Bolt = fast, clean frontend scaffolding for devs but no strategy layer or precision editing; Replit = coding control focus. Rocket's pitch is 'strategy + full-stack + continuous intelligence in one'. Independent comparisons (SourceForge/Slashdot) note Bolt is faster/simpler while Rocket claims cleaner architecture and scaling control. Sources: https://sourceforge.net/software/compare/Bolt.new-vs-Lovable-vs-Rocket.new/ , rocket.new blog
48	
49	=== #12 [IDEA/NORMAL] Weakness: mobile publishing is high-friction
50	["research"]
51	Flutter mobile apps can be downloaded as **APK for Android testing**, but **iOS requires downloading source code and building locally in Xcode** with an Apple Developer account ($99/yr); Google Play submission needs the one-time $25 fee. So 'build a mobile app from a prompt' still dumps non-technical users into native toolchains to actually ship. A real gap Kodely can either match honestly or improve. Source: https://docs.rocket.new/help/faq
52	
53	=== #13 [IDEA/NORMAL] Weakness: GitHub two-way sync limited to Next.js TS
54	["research"]
55	GitHub **two-way sync** (push to repo + pull external changes back in) is only supported for **Next.js TypeScript** projects, and **source-code download requires a paid plan (Pro+)**. Flutter/mobile and free-tier users are more locked in. Export limitations are a common lock-in grievance Kodely can differentiate on by offering full export earlier. Source: https://docs.rocket.new/help/faq
56	
57	=== #14 [IDEA/HIGH] Credit/token economics are opaque
58	["research"]
59	Neither the pricing page nor docs publish a **credit-to-action conversion** (how many messages/edits = 1 credit). Guidance is only qualitative ('clear prompts use fewer credits, vague ones use more'). Combined with the 'buy more credits' pressure, this opacity is a recurring trust complaint. Kodely can win goodwill with transparent, predictable usage metering. Source: https://docs.rocket.new/get-started/pricing-plans , https://docs.rocket.new/help/faq
60	
61	=== #15 [IDEA/LOW] Enterprise/compliance posture
62	["research"]
63	Rocket advertises SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, and CCPA compliance, plus SAML/SSO, audit logs, data localization, and premium support via a 'contact sales' enterprise track. This signals they're chasing upmarket/enterprise buyers alongside indie builders. Kodely should know the compliance bar for any enterprise-facing positioning. Source: https://www.rocket.new/build
64	
65	=== #16 [IDEA/NORMAL] Input sources beyond text: Figma, screenshot, Notion, Supabase
66	["research"]
67	Rocket accepts multiple 'starting points' to seed a build: **Figma frame imports** (layouts/components/tokens), **screenshot-to-code**, **Notion document conversion**, and **Supabase schema imports**. This design-to-app on-ramp targets designers and PMs, widening the funnel beyond pure prompters. A notable table-stakes surface area for Kodely to consider matching. Source: https://www.rocket.new/build
68	
69	=== #17 [IDEA/LOW] Content/SEO moat: heavy comparison-blog strategy
70	["research"]
71	Rocket runs an aggressive SEO play — a large blog of 'Rocket.new vs X pricing/comparison' articles (vs Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Base44, Emergent, Rork) plus 'best vibe coding prompts' listicles — all self-authored to capture bottom-funnel search. Kodely will face this branded-comparison SERP dominance and should plan its own comparison content early. Source: https://www.rocket.new/blog/
72	
73	=== #18 [IDEA/HIGH] Lovable — What it is & positioning
74	["research"]
75	Lovable (lovable.dev) is a Stockholm-based 'vibe coding' platform that turns natural-language chat into production-ready full-stack web apps and websites. It positions itself as the fastest idea-to-app tool for non-engineers and PMs, and evolved from the viral open-source GPT Engineer project (51k+ GitHub stars, 27k waitlist), rebranded to Lovable in Dec 2024. Founded Nov 2023 by CEO Anton Osika (ex-CERN) and CTO Fabian Hedin. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovable_(company) , https://research.contrary.com/company/lovable
76	
77	=== #19 [IDEA/HIGH] Lovable — Build workflow (prompt → app)
78	["research"]
79	You describe the app in chat; Lovable scaffolds UI, wires routing, and (with backend connected) generates DB schema, auth, RLS policies and edge functions from plain English. Lovable 2.0 (24 Apr 2025) split this into an autonomous Agent Mode (plans/debugs across steps, reads logs, queries DB) and a Chat Mode (planning without editing code). A CRUD app with auth reportedly costs 30–60 credits for the initial build. Sources: https://lovable.dev/blog/lovable-2-0 , https://www.nocode.mba/articles/lovable-ai-app-builder
80	
81	=== #20 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Lovable — Tech stack it outputs
82	["research"]
83	Lovable generates a standard, non-locked React + Vite + Tailwind CSS frontend with Supabase for backend (Postgres, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime). Exported projects have the normal folder structure any React dev expects and open in VS Code/Cursor. Note: it is frontend-React/Vite-first (not Next.js), a meaningful gap vs SSR/SEO-heavy use cases. Sources: https://lovable.dev/faq/code-export , https://vercel.com/i/v0-vs-lovable
84	
85	=== #21 [IDEA/HIGH] Lovable Cloud — managed backend (key differentiator)
86	["research"]
87	Lovable Cloud is a fully-managed Supabase instance provisioned automatically, giving Postgres, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions and Realtime with zero setup — the AI auto-generates schema, RLS and auth flows. The tradeoff: the project doesn't appear in your own Supabase dashboard and you don't get service-role keys or direct DB URLs (there's a community exporter to migrate off). Users can instead connect a self-managed Supabase via Settings → Connectors. Source: https://supabase.com/blog/lovable-cloud-launch , https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/identify-lovable-cloud-or-supabase-backend
88	
89	=== #22 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Lovable — Integrations (Supabase, GitHub, Stripe)
90	["research"]
91	First-class Supabase integration (auth, DB, storage, edge functions deployed automatically). Two-way GitHub/GitLab sync so edits flow both directions. Stripe payments are built via Supabase Edge Functions calling the Stripe API with secrets — e.g. prompting 'add a checkout button and process payments with Stripe.' Sources: https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/supabase , https://lovable.dev/faq/code-export
92	
93	=== #23 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Lovable — Deploy, custom domains & editing modes
94	["research"]
95	One-click publish with custom domains, transactional email from custom domains, plus a Visual Editor for click-to-edit UI changes (no prompt/credit needed) and a Dev Mode for direct code editing. A built-in Security Scan checks Supabase-backed apps for vulnerabilities (e.g. exposed RLS) at publish time. Sources: https://analyticsindiamag.com/ai-news-updates/lovable-launches-version-2-0-with-smarter-chat-agent-multiplayer-features-and-security-scan/ , https://lovable.dev/blog/lovable-2-0
96	
97	=== #24 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Lovable — Collaboration & Teams (multiplayer)
98	["research"]
99	Lovable 2.0 added real-time multiplayer editing. Pro users get personal workspaces with project collaborators; the Teams tier supports up to 20 members sharing a credit pool with centralized billing. Business ($50/mo) adds SSO, a security center and access controls. Source: https://www.testingcatalog.com/lovable-2-0-introduces-chat-mode-agent-alongside-multiplayer-support/
100	
101	=== #25 [CHORE/HIGH] Lovable — Exact pricing & credits (2026)
102	["research"]
103	Four tiers: Free ($0, 5 daily credits capped ~150/mo, reset 00:00 UTC, no rollover), Pro ($25/mo, 100 monthly credits + up to 5 daily), Business ($50/mo, 100 credits + SSO/security center), Enterprise (custom). Every AI message consumes credits and paid-plan credits roll over. Critically, runtime Lovable Cloud/AI usage is billed separately on top of subscription credits. Sources: https://www.eesel.ai/blog/lovable-pricing , https://www.nocode.mba/articles/lovable-pricing
104	
105	=== #26 [IDEA/NORMAL] Lovable — Code export & ownership
106	["research"]
107	Users own 100% of their code and keep it even after cancelling — no lock-in. Export by downloading a zip from the code editor or via two-way GitHub/GitLab sync; once on GitHub you can clone, version, and deploy anywhere independently. This clean-ownership story is a strong trust signal Kodely should match. Sources: https://lovable.dev/faq/code-export , https://vp0.com/blogs/does-lovable-own-my-code
108	
109	=== #27 [IDEA/NORMAL] Lovable — Company, funding & valuation
110	["research"]
111	One of the fastest-growing software companies ever. Series A $200M at $1.8B (early 2025), Series B $330M at $6.6B (Dec 2025), and a Series C of ~$400M at a $13.3B valuation announced Aug 2026 — total raised ~$550M+. Team ~146 (Feb 2026), deliberately staying Europe-based. Sources: https://techstartups.com/2026/08/12/swedish-vibe-coding-startup-lovable-raises-400-million-at-13-3-billion-valuation-as-arr-nears-600-million/ , https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2026/06/05/ai-coding-startup-lovable-in-talks-to-raise-funding-at-a-12-billion-valuation/
112	
113	=== #28 [IDEA/NORMAL] Lovable — Traction (ARR & users)
114	["research"]
115	ARR scaled from ~$200M (Nov 2025) to ~$500–600M by mid-2026 — roughly 2.5x in seven months (~14% MoM compounding), reaching $206M ARR in its first 11 months. User base reported at ~2.3M (early 2026). This growth curve is the headline reason the vibe-coding category is hot. Sources: https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/19/as-lovable-hits-200m-arr-its-ceo-credits-staying-in-europe-for-its-success , https://catalaize.substack.com/p/lovables-path-from-open-source-to
116	
117	=== #29 [BUG/HIGH] Lovable — Reviews & complaints
118	["research"]
119	Trustpilot has 1,000+ reviews polarized 64% 5-star / 17% 1-star. #1 complaint across Trustpilot/Reddit/G2 is unpredictable credit consumption — users get charged for the AI's own mistakes and describe it as 'a slot machine with credits.' The AI gets stuck in debugging loops (fixes one thing, breaks another). One user cited $1,000+ in underestimated API costs. Most-praised trait: raw speed to a working prototype. Sources: https://aitoolgrade.com/review/lovable.html , https://www.zite.com/blog/lovable-reviews
120	
121	=== #30 [IDEA/NORMAL] Lovable — Strengths & weaknesses summary
122	["research"]
123	Strengths: fastest prompt-to-prototype, clean React/Tailwind output, zero-setup managed backend (Lovable Cloud), true code ownership, security scan, multiplayer. Weaknesses: credit burn on the AI's own errors, debugging-loop degradation on complex apps ('promising start, non-functional messes'), frontend-only React/Vite (no Next.js/SSR), separate runtime bill, and self-hosted-Supabase friction. Sources: https://emergent.sh/learn/lovable-review , https://aitoolgrade.com/review/lovable.html
124	
125	=== #31 [IDEA/HIGH] Bolt.new — What it is & positioning
126	["research"]
127	Bolt.new (by StackBlitz) is an in-browser AI full-stack app builder that lets you prompt, run, edit and deploy apps entirely in the browser — positioned as more developer-leaning than Lovable, with a real Node.js runtime and terminal. Claude is the default model powering code generation. It hit 5M registered users by May 2025. Sources: https://github.com/stackblitz/bolt.new , https://sacra.com/c/bolt-new/
128	
129	=== #32 [IDEA/URGENT] Bolt.new — WebContainers live preview (moat)
130	["research"]
131	Bolt's core differentiator is StackBlitz WebContainers: a WebAssembly 'micro-OS' that runs a full Node.js environment client-side in the browser. Compilation, bundling, npm installs, terminal commands and preview all happen locally with no remote server, giving instant live preview and real backend execution. This is the standout technical asset a Kodely clone would find hardest to replicate. Sources: https://blog.khriztianmoreno.dev/en/posts/webcontainers-at-its-best-bolt-new-combines-ai-and-full-stack-development-in-the-browser , https://bytes.dev/archives/329
132	
133	=== #33 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Build workflow & tech output
134	["research"]
135	Prompt → Bolt generates React, Next.js, Vite, Vue, Astro, Svelte, Remix or plain Node projects and the WebContainer runs them in real time. It supports npm installs, filesystem ops and terminal commands in-sandbox, so it's more flexible on frameworks than Lovable's React/Vite-only output. Backends typically use Supabase or serverless API routes. Sources: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/what-is-bolt , https://vibe-eval.com/guides/bolt-base44-tech-stack/
136	
137	=== #34 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Integrations & Figma/Expo import
138	["research"]
139	Built-in integrations: Supabase, Stripe, GitHub, Netlify, plus Figma and Expo. Figma frames import into existing projects at any time (via Anima; 3 free conversions/mo then 50–200k tokens each). Expo integration exports to native iOS/Android from prompts with instant QR-code device preview — a mobile capability Lovable lacks. Sources: https://bolt.new/blog/import-figma-frames-into-existing-bolt-projects , https://expo.dev/ai/bolt
140	
141	=== #35 [FEATURE/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Deploy & custom domains
142	["research"]
143	One-click deploy from the browser to Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare; typical output is a static React SPA plus serverless functions. All paid plans include custom domains and remove Bolt branding. A recurring user complaint is the 'preview works, production breaks' gap due to environment differences. Sources: https://vibe-eval.com/guides/bolt-base44-tech-stack/ , https://www.nocode.mba/articles/bolt-pricing-2026
144	
145	=== #36 [CHORE/HIGH] Bolt.new — Exact pricing & tokens (2026)
146	["research"]
147	Token-metered. Free ($0): 1M tokens/mo, 300K daily cap, no card. Pro $25/mo (~10M tokens). Higher Pro tiers: Pro 50 = $50/mo/26M tokens, Pro 100 = $100/mo/55M, Pro 200 = $200/mo/120M. Teams $30/member/mo with admin controls; Enterprise custom. Since July 2025 unused tokens roll over one extra month; annual billing saves up to ~28%. Sources: https://www.nocode.mba/articles/bolt-pricing-2026 , https://costbench.com/software/ai-coding-assistants/bolt-new/
148	
149	=== #37 [IDEA/HIGH] Bolt.new — Open source (bolt.diy) & ownership
150	["research"]
151	bolt.diy is the official MIT-licensed open-source version (from StackBlitz Labs, started by Cole Medin) — self-hostable via local/Docker with a choice of 19+ LLM providers using your own API keys. This is strategically relevant: Kodely could fork/study bolt.diy rather than rebuild WebContainers from scratch. Users own and can export their code to GitHub. Sources: https://github.com/stackblitz-labs/bolt.diy , https://bolters.io/docs/versioning-open-source.html
152	
153	=== #38 [IDEA/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Company, funding & Microsoft deal
154	["research"]
155	StackBlitz raised a $105.5M Series B (Jan 2025, Emergence Capital + GV, with Greylock/Insight/Madrona), total funding ~$135M by Dec 2025 at a ~$700M valuation. In May 2026 Bolt partnered with Microsoft to run on Azure/M365 (Azure-native deploy, Microsoft Marketplace procurement, Teams/365 Copilot integration) — a partnership, not an acquisition. Sources: https://sacra.com/c/bolt-new/ , https://bolt.new/blog/news-press-release-bolt.new-on-microsoft-azure
156	
157	=== #39 [IDEA/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Traction (ARR & growth)
158	["research"]
159	Explosive early curve: ~$1M ARR in week one, $4M in 30 days, ~$20M in ~2 months, hitting $40M ARR by March 2025 — one of the fastest $0→$40M ramps on record. 5M registered users by May 2025. Growth later slowed relative to Lovable, but the launch remains a category benchmark. Sources: https://getlatka.com/companies/bolt.new , https://signalhub.substack.com/p/boltnew-arr-at-20m-in-just-2-months
160	
161	=== #40 [BUG/HIGH] Bolt.new — Reviews & complaints
162	["research"]
163	Reddit r/boltnewbuilders sentiment (Apr 2026) ~54% positive / 29% negative; Trustpilot a harsh 1.4/5. Dominant complaint: runaway token burn — every prompt re-reads the full codebase, and error loops can consume 7–12M tokens in an afternoon, with reviewers estimating ~half of tokens wasted on the AI fixing its own bugs (it rewrites whole files). Second: 'preview works, production breaks.' Praised for dev-grade flexibility and speed. Sources: https://www.yeasitech.com/bolt-new-problems-solutions , https://superdesign.dev/blog/bolt-review
164	
165	=== #41 [IDEA/NORMAL] Bolt.new — Strengths & weaknesses summary
166	["research"]
167	Strengths: real in-browser Node runtime (WebContainers), multi-framework output incl. Next.js, Figma & Expo/mobile, generous free tier, token rollover, open-source bolt.diy, enterprise Azure path. Weaknesses: severe token burn on complex/error-loop sessions, full-codebase re-reads inflate cost, prod/preview drift, WebContainer memory limits on large apps, and a more developer-oriented (less polished no-code) UX than Lovable. Sources: https://aiunpacking.com/review/bolt-new/ , https://www.banani.co/blog/bolt-new-pricing
168	
169	=== #42 [IDEA/HIGH] v0: Positioning & workflow
170	["research"]
171	v0 (v0.dev, now v0.app) is Vercel's AI product for building web UIs and, since early 2026, full apps via a chat-first workflow: you prompt in natural language, v0 streams a live React preview, and you iterate by chatting, editing visually, or editing code. It targets developers and designers who want production-grade front-end fast. In Feb 2026 Vercel expanded it from a UI generator into a broader platform with Git integration, a VS Code-style editor, database connectivity, and agentic multi-step workflows. Sources: https://www.nxcode.io/resources/news/v0-by-vercel-complete-guide-2026 , https://v0.app/docs/faqs
172	
173	=== #43 [IDEA/HIGH] v0: What it generates (React/Next/shadcn/Tailwind)
174	["research"]
175	v0 outputs clean, idiomatic React and Next.js code using shadcn/ui components and Tailwind CSS — widely regarded as the highest-quality code output among AI builders. It is deliberately opinionated toward the modern Vercel/Next stack. This is both its strength (excellent front-end fidelity) and its lock-in: if you use Vue, Svelte, or deploy on AWS/GCP, v0 is a poor fit. Sources: https://superdesign.dev/blog/v0-review , https://www.taskade.com/blog/v0-review
176	
177	=== #44 [FEATURE/HIGH] v0: Design Mode + Figma import + visual editing
178	["research"]
179	Design Mode lets users click any element in the live preview and edit layout, copy, spacing, and styling visually without regenerating from scratch — a key differentiator vs pure chat tools. Premium plans add Figma import: bring an existing Figma design in and generate matching React/shadcn code, bridging designer-developer handoff. This tri-modal editing (chat + visual + code) is central to v0's UX. Sources: https://vercel.com/blog/working-with-figma-and-custom-design-systems-in-v0 , https://superdesign.dev/blog/v0-review
180	
181	=== #45 [IDEA/HIGH] v0: Pricing & token-based credits
182	["research"]
183	5 tiers (2026): Free $0 ($5/mo credits), Premium $20/mo ($20 credits, Figma import, API, buy-more), Team $30/user/mo (shared credits, SSO-ish collab), Business $100/user/mo, Enterprise custom. In Feb 2026 v0 moved from fixed credit counts to token-based pricing — each generation costs variable tokens by complexity, so real cost tracks how much you build. A complex prompt can burn 5 credits at once; heavy iteration on one component can eat 15–20 credits — a top user complaint about unpredictability. Sources: https://uibakery.io/blog/vercel-v0-pricing-explained-what-you-get-and-how-it-compares , https://superdesign.dev/blog/v0-review
184	
185	=== #46 [FEATURE/NORMAL] v0: Export, ownership & GitHub/Vercel integration
186	["research"]

# Kodely — Competitive Position

Synthesis of the 99 cards in the board's "Competitor Teardowns" column, checked
against what `kodely-prod` actually does today and against competitor pricing
re-verified on 2026-08-22.

**Scope discipline.** Every claim about Kodely below cites the code that backs
it. Every claim about a competitor is either verified against a primary source
on 2026-08-22 or explicitly marked unverified. Where a board card is now wrong,
it is listed in [§6](#6-board-cards-that-are-stale-or-wrong).

---

## 1. What Kodely actually is

Not a summary of the marketing — a summary of the code.

Kodely generates **one Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind single-page app**,
compiles it server-side, and serves the compiled output from its own
infrastructure under a CSP that blocks every external host.

| Dimension | Reality | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Output | One SPA. "Build distinct sections/routes as components conditionally rendered or scrolled to, not separate .html files." | `lib/agent.ts:51` |
| Dependencies | `react` + `react-dom` only. The agent cannot add packages; there is no per-generation install step. | `lib/foundation.ts:16-19`, `lib/agent.ts:55-57` |
| Backend | None. No DB, no auth, no API, no server functions for the generated site. | `prisma/schema.prisma` has no generated-app models; `lib/foundation.ts` |
| Network | `connect-src 'none'`. No fetch, no XHR, no CDN, no remote images, no web fonts. | `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:28-29` |
| Forms | Explicitly forbidden to build one that appears functional. Uses `mailto:` / `tel:` / bracketed link-outs instead. | `lib/agent.ts:92-101` |
| Images | Inline SVG, CSS gradients, `data:` URIs, and a ~460-item built-in catalogue. No uploads, no stock. | `lib/agent.ts:58-63` |
| Hosting | First-party. Published at `https://<slug>.kodely.site` behind Cloudflare. | `proxy.ts:33-34`, `lib/site-seo.ts:30-53` |
| Custom domains | **None.** Zero occurrences of `customDomain` / `cname` anywhere in `lib/`, `app/`, or `prisma/`. | grep, 2026-08-22 |
| Model | `claude-sonnet-5` at `high` effort for a first build, `medium` for an edit. Max 8 agent turns. | `lib/models.ts:12-34`, `lib/agent.ts:299` |
| Billing | One-time credit packs. **Not a subscription.** | `app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:37` (`mode: "payment"`) |

The template gallery has already made a market choice the rest of the board has
not caught up to. Its seven categories are *Food & drink, Beauty & wellness,
Local services, Professional services, Personal & creative, Startup & product,
Events & causes* (`lib/templates.ts:26-33`) — local businesses and personal
sites, not the "non-technical founder building an MVP" that the board's
**Market & Users** column assumes. See [§5, Choice 3](#choice-3-name-the-market-brochure-site-not-app).

---

## 2. Where Kodely genuinely wins today

These are real, code-backed, and — against the verified competitor set — mostly
unmatched. They are also all in the same family: **honesty about money and
about what was actually shipped.**

### 2.1 It is the only pay-once product in the category

`app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:37` uses Stripe `mode: "payment"`. The packs
in `lib/stripe.ts:44-48` are one-time purchases, and `CreditLedger`
(`prisma/schema.prisma:275-287`) has no expiry column — the `/pricing` page's
claim that "Credits never expire" is backed by the schema, not by policy.

Verified 2026-08-22, every major rival is subscription-gated:

| Product | Cheapest paid plan | Can you buy credits without a subscription? |
|---|---|---|
| Lovable | Pro $20–25/mo *(sources conflict)* | No — top-ups require an active Pro/Business plan |
| Bolt.new | Pro $25/mo | No — purchased and rolled-over tokens need an active sub |
| v0 | Plus $30/user/mo (Premium $20 closed to new users) | No — Premium/Plus/Business only |
| Replit | Core $20/mo annual, $25/mo monthly | No — pay-as-you-go sits on top of a plan |
| Base44 | Starter $16/mo (annualized) | Top-ups tied to an existing plan |
| Rocket.new | Pro $25/mo | No — docs state an active paid subscription is required |
| Hostinger Horizons | Explorer $6.99/mo annual ($9.99 monthly) | Closest: support doc states top-ups "don't require an additional subscription" — but still presumes a Hostinger plan |

There is no true pay-once, no-recurring-fee credit pack in this market. Kodely's
$9 starter pack is a genuinely differentiated commercial shape. Whether it is
*sized* correctly is a separate and serious problem — see [§4](#4-the-pricing-landscape-and-where-kodely-sits).

### 2.2 A credit is a published dollar amount, not a mystery unit

`lib/credits.ts:12` — `MICROS_PER_CREDIT = 2_000`. One credit is $0.002 of real
model spend. Charge is computed from **metered tokens after the fact**
(`costMicros`, `lib/credits.ts:38-47`), never from a flat guess.

The category's single loudest complaint is the opposite of this. Board cards
document it across five vendors: Rocket publishes no credit-to-action
conversion at all (card #14); Bubble's Workload Units draw the loudest
complaints in no-code (card #76); Replit shows the exact price only *after* the
Agent finishes (card #51); Lovable users describe it as "a slot machine with
credits" (card #29); Bolt reviewers estimate roughly half of tokens go to the
AI fixing its own bugs (card #40).

Hostinger has since moved the same direction Kodely already sits — as of June
2026 Horizons meters *dynamic credits* by computing resources consumed, not
flat per-message (verified: Hostinger support doc 11136677). That is
convergence on Kodely's model, which is a validation of the design and an
erosion of the differentiator at the same time.

### 2.3 A failed build is free, and "failed" is decided by a compiler

`app/api/generate/route.ts:325` writes `creditsCharged: 0` on failure. What
makes this stronger than a policy promise is the definition of success:
`buildSite()` (`lib/build-site.ts:25-60`) runs a real `vite build` in a
throwaway directory against a pre-installed foundation tree, and only output
that compiles is stored and charged.

**Honest caveat.** If the *repair* pass succeeds, the user pays for both passes
— `app/api/generate/route.ts:259-260` charges the token totals accumulated
across every turn, repairs included. Only a build that never compiles at all is
free. Marketing must say "a build that fails is free," not "we never charge you
for our mistakes"; the second claim is not true as written.

### 2.4 Preview and production are byte-identical

The CSP string in `app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts:16-17` and
`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:28-29` is the same string, and both
routes serve compiled artefacts from `ProjectFile`. There is no separate
runtime, no WebContainer, no dev-server-versus-build divergence.

This structurally eliminates a complaint that appears against two competitors
in the board's own research: "preview works, production breaks" is listed as a
recurring Bolt grievance in cards #35 and #40. Kodely cannot have that bug,
because the preview *is* the build output.

### 2.5 A user-set spend cap, enforced before anything is spent

`getSpendCapStatus` (`lib/credits.ts:154-189`) tracks a rolling-30-day ceiling
the user sets themselves; `app/api/generate/route.ts:59-72` checks it before a
single token is spent and returns a 402 explaining that *the user* set the
limit.

No competitor in the 99 cards is documented as offering this. It is the exact
control that the incidents the board catalogued would have needed: $607 over a
$25/mo Replit plan in 3.5 days, $1,982 in 24 days on a pre-launch app
(**Market & Users**, "Churn driver #2"), $250 on Rocket credits (card #7),
$1,000+ in underestimated Lovable costs (card #29).

### 2.6 Full source export, free and ungated

`app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts` has no plan check, no credit charge,
and no tier gate — any signed-in owner gets the complete Vite + React + TS
source tree as a zip. It is wired into the editor UI at
`app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx:304-327`.

Verified 2026-08-22: Rocket.new's own docs still state source download
"requires a paid plan (Pro or above)" — card #13 holds. GoDaddy Airo goes
further the other way and requires a **paid plan to publish at all**.

*(The task brief described export as "built but not deployed." The route and its
UI entry point both exist in the tree; whether the currently deployed build
includes them is a deployment question this analysis did not verify.)*

### 2.7 A free, unbilled plan step before spending

`lib/enhance.ts` expands a one-line prompt into an editable spec on
`claude-haiku-4-5`, deliberately unbilled and not recorded as a build. Its
header comment states the reasoning directly: "a preview you pay for is not a
preview." The abuse ceiling is rate-limiting, not the credit meter.

The board's **Differentiation & Moat** column lists "'Plan/Chat mode' before
spending credits" as an aspiration. It already ships.

### 2.8 The sandbox is enforced in headers and path rules, not in the prompt

Two layers, both real access controls rather than instructions:

- `connect-src 'none'` in the served CSP means a generated page cannot call
  out, exfiltrate, or load a tracker even if a prompt talked the model into
  writing one.
- `PROTECTED_PATHS` / `PROTECTED_PATTERNS` / `normalizePath`
  (`lib/agent.ts:176-204`) refuse writes to `vite.config.ts`, `package.json`,
  `tsconfig.json`, and all dotfiles. The comment is explicit about why: the
  Vite config is *executed* server-side, so "a sentence in the system prompt is
  not an access control."

This is the correct reading of the Replit production-database incident (card
#53), whose lesson the card itself states precisely: the code freeze lived only
in instructions, and nothing in the execution path enforced it. Kodely's
equivalent guard is in the execution path.

### 2.9 It refuses to fabricate facts about a real business

`lib/agent.ts:74-90` forbids inventing addresses, phone numbers, opening hours,
prices, staff names, certifications, review scores, or testimonials, and
explicitly ranks this *above* the "no placeholder text" rule. The reasoning in
the prompt is the right one: an invented phone number is a real number
belonging to somebody else.

For the local-business market the template gallery actually targets, this is a
sharper trust story than any generic "production-ready code" claim, and none of
the 99 cards records a competitor making it.

---

## 3. Where Kodely structurally cannot compete

The distinction that matters: these are not missing features on a roadmap. Each
one is blocked by an architectural commitment that the current foundation
cannot reach incrementally.

### 3.1 The entire "app" market — closed

Lovable, Replit, Base44, Bolt, Rocket, and Chef all generate a database, auth,
and server logic. Kodely's generated projects have `react` and `react-dom`
(`lib/foundation.ts:16-19`), and `lib/build-site.ts:12-26` builds against a
single shared, pre-installed foundation tree specifically so that no build ever
runs `npm install`. That property is what makes server-side compilation safe to
run at all.

**What would have to change:** per-project dependency installation, a sandboxed
runtime, a provisioned database, an auth service, and a secrets store. That is
not a feature — it is a different product with a different security model. The
board's **Differentiation & Moat** card "Real backend, DB & auth built-in" is
not reachable from this foundation, and should be re-scoped or retired rather
than left standing as a moat.

### 3.2 Multi-page sites — closed by prompt, and it is the common case

`lib/agent.ts:51` mandates a single-page app. Most SMB brochure sites are
multi-page (Home / Services / About / Contact). This is the gap that hurts most
*within* the market Kodely has actually chosen, and unlike §3.1 it is
reachable: a router plus multiple HTML entry points is a foundation change, not
an architecture change. The serving route already handles arbitrary paths and
already synthesises a sitemap over every `.html` file it finds
(`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:64-72`) — the serving layer is ready
for multi-page before the generator is.

### 3.3 A form that delivers — closed, and it is the #1 SMB job-to-be-done

The prompt forbids any form that appears functional (`lib/agent.ts:92-101`),
and the reasoning is correct — a form that silently discards a real enquiry is
worse than no form. But lead capture is the main commercial reason a local
business wants a website. A `mailto:` link is a materially worse answer, and
every hosting-company competitor bundles a real one.

This is the cheapest high-value gap on the list: a Kodely-hosted form endpoint
that emails the site owner requires no change to the generated app's
architecture, only a CSP carve-out for a single first-party origin and an
endpoint on Kodely's own infrastructure. `lib/mail.ts` already exists.

### 3.4 Custom domains — absent, and it is the competitors' whole wedge

No `customDomain`, `cname`, or equivalent anywhere in the codebase. Sites live
at `<slug>.kodely.site`.

Hostinger Horizons bundles hosting on every tier plus a free domain for a year
from Starter up, and free mailboxes (verified 2026-08-22). Card #63 correctly
names Hostinger the closest strategic analog. A business will not run its
public presence on someone else's subdomain, so today Kodely produces a *draft*
of a website rather than a website — and the board's own **Pricing** column
already identifies "deploy/hosting/custom-domain as the natural upsell fence."
The fence exists; the gate does not.

### 3.5 Real photographs — absent, and for several template categories the photo is the product

Assets are inline SVG, gradients, and a ~460-item catalogue (`lib/agent.ts:58-63`);
`img-src 'self' data:` permits data URIs but there is no upload path for the
generated site. For *Food & drink* and *Beauty & wellness* — two of the seven
template categories — a site without the owner's photographs is not a
competitive artefact regardless of how well it is designed.

### 3.6 Every third-party embed — closed by `connect-src 'none'`

No analytics, no Calendly, no Google Maps, no chat widget, no booking embed, no
review widget, no payment button. This is the direct cost of §2.8. It is a
coherent trade, but it is currently an *unnamed* trade — see
[§5, Choice 4](#choice-4-decide-whether-the-sandbox-is-a-product-or-a-limitation).

### 3.7 Speed

The one recorded eval run
(`scripts/eval/results/2026-08-21T17-44-48-482Z-verify.json`) shows a
first build at **243 seconds** wall time against `maxDuration = 300` in
`app/api/generate/route.ts:11`. Four minutes to a first site, with 19% headroom
before the route ceiling. "Fastest prompt-to-prototype" is Lovable's
most-praised trait per card #30; that competitive axis is not currently winnable
and the timeout headroom is thin enough to be an operational risk on a larger
brief.

### 3.8 Teams, collaboration, GitHub sync

No collaboration models in `prisma/schema.prisma`; export is a manual zip
download, not two-way Git sync. Lovable, Bolt, v0, and Rocket all ship Git
integration. For the local-business market this matters far less than §3.2–3.5,
and it should be explicitly deprioritised rather than left as an open gap.

---

## 4. The pricing landscape and where Kodely sits

### 4.1 The packs and their margin

From `lib/stripe.ts:44-48`, against the $0.002/credit cost basis in
`lib/credits.ts:12`:

| Pack | Credits | Price | Per credit | Cost basis | Gross margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| starter | 500 | $9 | $0.0180 | $1.00 | 88.9% |
| builder | 2,500 | $40 | $0.0160 | $5.00 | 87.5% |
| pro | 6,000 | $90 | $0.0150 | $12.00 | 86.7% |

The margin is real and healthy. The volume discount is per-credit against the
starter pack, and margin drifts down slightly as the discount deepens — the
intended shape, and `lib/stripe.ts:22-43` documents it correctly after a
correction on 2026-08-22.

### 4.2 The problem the margin table hides

The margin is per *credit*. The customer buys *builds*. Translating:

Measured build cost is **144 credits** (2026-08-17) and **472 credits**
(2026-08-21 eval, `scripts/eval/results/`). `estimateCredits`
(`lib/credits.ts:115-117`) quotes 120–550 for a create and 60–300 for an edit,
deliberately wide because two samples is not a distribution.

At the measured 472-credit build:

| Pack | Builds it buys | Effective price per build |
|---|---|---|
| starter $9 | **1.06** | $8.50 |
| builder $40 | 5.3 | $7.55 |
| pro $90 | 12.7 | $7.08 |

At the optimistic 144-credit end, starter buys 3.5 builds at $2.59 each. **The
true answer is somewhere in a 3x band and nobody knows where.** `lib/credits.ts`
and `lib/stripe.ts` both carry explicit comments saying not to publish a
per-build price until `scripts/eval` has run a full sweep. That sweep has run
**once, against one prompt** (`selectedIds: ["plumber"]`, `count: 1`).

Three numbers that follow from this and are currently incoherent:

1. **The signup grant exceeds the starter pack.** `SIGNUP_GRANT = 750`
   (`lib/credits.ts:20`) versus a 500-credit starter pack. A new account is
   given 50% more credits than $9 buys. At 472 credits/build that is ~1.6 free
   builds handed to every signup, costing $1.50 of real model spend each, with
   no obvious reason to then buy the smallest pack.
2. **The social reward is below the noise floor.** `REWARD_CREDITS = 50`
   (`app/api/rewards/_lib.ts:26`) is roughly one tenth of a build — $0.10 of
   spend. It cannot buy anything the user can perceive.
3. **The headline number does not communicate.** "500 credits" reads generous
   and means about one website. Competitors' units are coarser and therefore
   more honest to a buyer: Lovable Pro is 100 credits, Rocket Pro is 100
   credits, Framer Basic is 1,000 AI credits. A Kodely credit is denominated at
   1/10th of a cent, so the number on the pack is an order of magnitude larger
   than the number of things it buys.

### 4.3 Where the $9 pack actually lands

Verified competitor entry points, 2026-08-22:

| Product | Entry | Commitment | Bundled |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kodely starter** | **$9 one-time** | **None** | Hosting on `*.kodely.site` |
| Hostinger Horizons Explorer | $6.99/mo annual ($9.99 monthly) | Annual for the low price | Hosting; domain from Starter up; mailboxes |
| Base44 Starter | $16/mo annualized | Subscription | Hosting, backend, auth |
| Lovable Pro | $20–25/mo *(unresolved)* | Subscription | Hosting, Cloud backend |
| Replit Core | $20/mo annual, $25 monthly | Subscription | Hosting, DB, auth, deploys |
| Bolt Pro | $25/mo | Subscription | Deploy to Netlify/Vercel/CF |
| v0 Plus | $30/user/mo | Subscription | Vercel deploy |

Kodely is the cheapest way to get *one* website with no recurring commitment,
and the only no-commitment option at all. It is *not* the cheapest way to get
volume: at $9.99/month Hostinger Horizons bundles hosting, mailboxes, and a
credit allowance for a whole month, and its dynamic credits meter the same way
Kodely's do.

**The positioning that survives contact with these numbers is "pay once, own
it, no subscription" — not "cheap."** The margin analysis says Kodely can
afford to be either; the pack sizing currently says neither clearly.

---

## 5. The strategic choices this forces

Five. Each is a fork, not a task.

- **Keep the unit, change the story.** Stop selling "credits" in the headline

  absence. It also pairs naturally with §2.9.
- **Carve a controlled allowlist.** A first-party form endpoint and a named set
  of embeds, with the CSP widened per-origin rather than opened.

form endpoint (§3.3) is compatible with *either* position, because the allowed
origin is Kodely's own.

## 7. Summary

**Where Kodely wins:** billing honesty that is enforced in code rather than
promised in copy — pay-once packs with no subscription and no expiry, a credit
denominated in published dollars, a compiler deciding what counts as a
deliverable, a user-set spend cap, free ungated source export, and a sandbox
whose guarantees are headers and path rules rather than prompt text.

**Where it cannot compete:** anything requiring a backend, a second page, a
working form, a custom domain, the owner's photographs, or a third-party embed
— and it will not win on speed.

**What that combination is:** the most trustworthy way to buy a single-page
website outright. That is a real position. It is not the position the board's
Market & Users column describes, and closing that gap is Choice 3.

content.text:
Both deliverables are written. The pre-existing modified/untracked files in `kodely-prod` were already there — my only addition is `docs/research/`. `board.sqlite` was opened read-only and its mtime is unchanged.

## Report

**Kodely's real defensible position, in two sentences:** Kodely is the only product in the category you can buy without a subscription — one-time credit packs (Stripe `mode: "payment"`), credits denominated in published dollars ($0.002 each), never expiring, with a compiler rather than a judgement call deciding whether you get charged, a user-set spend cap enforced pre-flight, free rollback to any prior build, and ungated free source export. Everything it wins on is honesty about money and about what was actually shipped; everything it loses on follows from one architectural commitment — `react` + `react-dom` only, no `npm install` per build — which closes the entire app market and cannot be reopened incrementally.

**The 3–5 forced strategic choices:**
1. **Name the market: single-page sites for local businesses, not apps.** The 23 template prompts already made this choice; the board's Market & Users column hasn't. Backend/DB/auth is not reachable from this foundation, so that moat card should be retired rather than left standing.
2. **Re-denominate the credit, or stop selling credits in the headline.** A credit is 1/10th of a cent, so "500 credits" reads generous and means about one website. Blocked on running the eval sweep — it has run once, against one prompt.
3. **The 750 signup grant and the 500-credit starter pack cannot both stand.** A new account is handed 50% more credits than $9 buys; the cheapest pack is dominated by the free tier.
4. **Decide whether the sandbox is a product or a limitation** — market `connect-src 'none'` as a privacy/no-trackers feature, or carve a controlled allowlist. Either way it is gated on closing two open audit findings.
5. **Cut the teardown column to competitors Kodely actually competes with** — Hostinger, GoDaddy Airo, Durable, Squarespace, Wix, Framer.

**Stale/wrong cards found: 24 of 99**, in four groups — 9 wrong on verified facts (Lovable's free tier and its now-unified Cloud billing, Hostinger's switch from message- to credit-metering, Framer's non-existent Scale tier, v0's sunset Premium tier, Replit's monthly price, #87's superseded ARR figures, #64's missing "publishing requires a paid plan", #62/#79 on Base44); 7 carrying a misapplied RECONCILE stamp (#88–#94); 4 describing a product that can no longer be signed up for (Firebase Studio #56/#57/#58/#61); and 4 that are research requests rather than findings (#95–#98). Roughly a dozen more are about products out of scope entirely if choice 1 lands.

**Cards written: 25** (the cap), all decisions or actions with reasoning in the description — 6 URGENT, 11 HIGH, 7 NORMAL, 1 LOW.

**Two findings worth flagging directly, both of which changed my conclusions mid-analysis:**
- I had to walk back a claim. `connect-src 'none'` blocks scripted requests, but `form-action` and `base-uri` are unset, so a generated page **can** POST to any external host — and `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` H1 (no `Host` check on the site route) is still open, meaning generated HTML is servable on the app origin. The sandbox is a real differentiator but must not be marketed in its absolute form until both are closed.
- **Signup has no rate limit and no email verification**, while granting 750 credits ($1.50 of real model spend) plus a server-side compile. An unverified email is currently worth up to 950 credits. That is an unpriced charge against the 87–89% margin the pricing model assumes.
